|Raw Variable Name| Clean Variable Name | Data Type| Numerical or Categorical | Description & Units |
|:--- | :--- |:--- | :--- |:--- |
|**Date**| date | chr | categorical | date in year-month-day format |
|**Rented Bike Count**| rented_bike_count | dbl | numerical | count of bikes rented at each hour |
|**Hour**| hour | dbl | numerical | hour of the day |
|**Temperature**| temperature_c | dbl | numerical | temperature in Celsius |
|**Humidity**| humidity_percent | dbl | numerical | humidity in percentage |
|**Wind Speed**| wind_speed_m_s | dbl | numerical | wind speed in m/s |
|**Visibility**| visibility_10m | dbl | numerical | visibility in 10m units |
|**Dew Point Temperature**| dew_point_temperature_c | dbl | numerical | dew point temperature - temperature at which the air needs to be cooled to (at constant pressure) in order to achieve a relative humidity |
|**Solar Radiation**| solar_radiation_mj_m2 | dbl | numerical | solar radiation in MJ/M^2 |
|**Rainfall**| rainfall_mm | dbl | numerical | rainfall in mm |
|**Snowfall**| snowfall_cm | dbl | numerical | snowfall in cm |
|**Seasons**| seasons | chr | categorical | represents the four seasons |
|**Holiday**| holiday | chr | categorical | holiday or no holiday |
|**Functioning Day**| functioning_day | chr | categorical | yes or no; represents if system is fully operational or not (will be cleaned away)|

## Questions
1. Does temperature affect bike demand differently during peak commuting hours (8-9am and 6-7pm) compared to off-peak hours? \
2. Is the holiday effect uniform across seasons, or do holiday demand patterns shift significantly between the seasons? \
3. Is there a sharp threshold or non-linear drop-off point where precipitation severly degrades demand, or is the decay linear? \
4. How do temperature and humidity combine to affect demand (compared to just considering temperature)? \
5. How does the hourly distribution shift between a regular working day and a non-working day?

## Loading and Cleaning Data
```{r load-data}
# load data 
seoul_bikes_raw <- read_csv("data/SeoulBikeData.csv", locale=locale(encoding="latin1"))
#extracting raw data, locale needed to be specified as error otherwise.

#clean data
seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes_raw |> 
  clean_names()
#cleaning names to snake_case, as column headings' words initially separated with space

#looking above at the variable table, it might mean that on non-functional days, there will be no bikes rented whatsoever. We run the following code to verify:
#seoul_bikes |> filter(functioning_day == "No" & rented_bike_count > 0)

seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes |> 
  filter(functioning_day != "No") |>  
  subset(select = -functioning_day)
#after dropping non-functioning days, we can drop the functioning_day variable entirely, as it has become redundant.
```

## Task 1 - Investigating the Effect of Temperature of Number of Rented Bikes During Peak or Non-Peak Hours

### 1.1 Data Wrangling

We define peak commuting hours as 7-9am and 5-7pm
```{r}
#Task 1
seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes |> 
  mutate(
    peak = ifelse(hour %in% c(7:9, 17:19), TRUE, FALSE)
    #used Gemini to help with shortening the conditional statement, as initially was hour == 7 | hour == 8 | ... 
  )
```

### 1.2a Data Visualisation (Scatterplot)

```{r}
#Task 1 - evaluating temperature sensitivty during peak hours vs. off-peak hours
seoul_bikes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = temperature_c, y = rented_bike_count)) +
  geom_jitter(
    aes(colour = peak),
    alpha = 0.15
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "gam",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.2,
    colour = "#d95f02"
    ) +
  facet_grid( #changed to facet_grid to take holidays into account, not taking weekdays vs. weekends into account as there many weekend workers in Seoul who may need to commute
    holiday ~ peak,
    labeller = as_labeller(c("TRUE" = "Peak", "FALSE" = "Non-Peak", "Holiday" = "Holiday", "No Holiday" = "Working Day"))
    ) +
  #changes labels from facetting to "Peak" and "Non-Peak"
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    guide = "legend",
    values = c("TRUE" = "#384860", "FALSE" = "#97a6c4"), #changed colour to lighter shades, as otherwise points are too dark
    labels = c("TRUE" = "Peak", "FALSE" = "Non-Peak")
    ) +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Temperature (c)",
    y = "Number of Rented Bikes Per Hour",
    colour = "Peak Commuting Hour (7-9am or 5-7pm)",
    title = "Bike Demand Sensitivity to Temperature"
  )
```

From the difference in the opacities/ darkness of each scatterplot, we can see that the dataset contains many more entries for non-peak hours than peak hours.

We can also see this from the following code:

```{r}
seoul_bikes |> 
  group_by(peak) |> 
  count()
```

However, we can already see there might be similarities in the pattern or the shape of the data represented above, where unimodal, asymmetric clusters can be seen for the two groups.

From the points during peak commuting hours, we see its maximum is much higher than that of the non-peak hours, the values specifically are 3556 vs. 2579 bikes/ hour.

On average, we also see that the number of rented bikes per hour is significantly higher during peak hours, with the means being approx. 1052 vs. 621, and the medians being 867 vs. 440.

The spread of data between peak and non-peak hours are also quite different, where the standard deviation for peak and non-peak hours are approx. 798 vs. 540 bikes/ hour and the interquartile range being approx 1290 vs. 772. This may suggest that the number of bikes that are rented during off peak times might be less predictable or less stable. However, it must also be noted that we have not removed holidays from this plot, so the peak hours may also include weekends and holidays, where no work is conducted. The spread of data exclusively on working days may be less spread out for peak times in particular.

Additionally, if we consider the GAM line on the scatterplot, we see that the line for the peak hours are much steeper than that of the non-peak hours, which may suggest that temperature acts as a stronger multiplier during peak hours.

We also see that the resiliance of commuters during lower temperatures (colder weather) at peak times is stronger, this would imply that commuters are less likely to not commute with bikes, as they must get to work or get to school on time. Conversely, for those during off-peak hours, the lower coldness tolerance may suggest they are less reliant on renting bikes and may choose to stay indoors or opt for another form of transport entirely.

Back to the similarities, we see that at high heat, the number of rented bikes per hour drop off. This means that once a threshold of around 30 degrees C is hit, even the peak commuters will choose another way of commuting, likely travelling with transportation offerring air-conditioning, e.g. busses or the metro.
```{r}
seoul_bikes |> 
  group_by(peak) |> 
  summarise(
    max = max(rented_bike_count),
    min = min(rented_bike_count),
    mean = mean(rented_bike_count),
    median = median(rented_bike_count),
    sd = sd(rented_bike_count),
    iqr = IQR(rented_bike_count)
  )
```

To be more specific, we shall analyse the distribution of the data, we should instead consider the density plots:
```{r}
determine_density_maxes <- function(df, max_var, max_var_condition, density_var){ #parameters to keep generality of function
  density_df <- df |>
    filter({{ max_var }} == max_var_condition) |>
    pull({{ density_var }}) |> 
    density() |> 
    (\(d) tibble::tibble(x = d$x, y = d$y))()
    #creating a separate data frame for density values
  
    high_peak <- density_df |> filter(y == max(y))
    low_peak <- density_df |> filter(x < 15) |> filter(y == max(y))
    
    tibble::tibble(
      max_y_high = high_peak$y,
      x_at_max_y_high = high_peak$x,
      max_y_low = low_peak$y,
      x_at_max_y_low = low_peak$x
    )
    #returns values in tibble form
    
}
#needed to use {{}} as passing in the column names and not variable objects - Gemini was used, as it was initially causing errors

peak_maxes<- determine_density_maxes(seoul_bikes, peak, TRUE, temperature_c)
non_peak_maxes <- determine_density_maxes(seoul_bikes, peak, FALSE, temperature_c)

peak_maxes
non_peak_maxes

#followed the following guide: https://ianmadd.github.io/pages/PeakDensityDistribution.html

seoul_bikes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = temperature_c, alpha = 0.1, colour = ifelse(peak == TRUE, "#384860", "#97a6c4"))) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_high, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#384860") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_low, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#384860") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = non_peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_high, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#97a6c4") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = non_peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_low, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#97a6c4") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_colour_identity(
    guide = "legend",
    labels = c("Peak", "Non-Peak")
    ) +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Temperature (c)",
    y = "Density",
    colour = "Peak Commuting Hour (8-9am or 6-7pm)",
    title = stringr::str_wrap("Temperature Distribution Comparison : Peak and Non-Peak Commuting Hours")
    #needed str_wrap to ensure the entire title shows on the plot
  )
```

Just looking at the shape of the curves, they are both clearly bimodal (i.e. two distinct peaks) and at specific points. Each peak in each of the density plots are highlighted by the vertical dashed or dotted line passing through them, with the corresponding colours matching if it is for the peak times or non-peak times plots.

We can see that both plots resemble the same shape, essentially an "M", where the right peak is slightly higher than the one on the left.

This may indicate how the relative proportions of how bike-renters reacting to changes in temperatures are almost identical across peak and off-peak commuting hours.

From the peaks of the density plots, we may also infer that bike-renters (unsurprisingly) are not immune to changes in temperatures (and thereby weather). For example when it is hot at close to 30 degrees C, the proportion of bike renters fall at a much quicker rate across both time windows. When it is colder, we see how when temperatures are colder than approximately -5 degrees C, the proportion of bike renters also fall more quickly. Most interesting is the middle of the peaks where the trough lies, as the number of falls at approximately 13 degrees C. This is likely due to the fact that Seoul as a city in general experiences long, cold winters and long, warm summers, hence the number of data entries are perceived are lower.

# 2.1 Grouping data by rented bike count holiday vs no holiday
```{r}
holiday_comparison <- seoul_bikes %>%
  group_by(holiday) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_rentals = mean(rented_bike_count, na.rm = TRUE),
   )
```

#2.2 Bar chart of rented bike count holiday vs no holiday
```{r}
ggplot(holiday_comparison,
       aes(x = holiday, y = avg_rentals, fill = holiday)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Average bike rentals during a holiday vs non-holiday",
    x = "Holiday vs Non-Holiday",
    y = "Average number of bikes rented"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Observations: Very simple bar chart and code shows that on average there is more bike rentals during non-holiday days vs holiday days. Is this suprising? For me it was slightly suprising (presuming this is seouls holiday) you might have thought people get out and about explore the city more, if tourists come over you definetly might presume they rent out bikes. On the contrary many workers may leave the city for the holiday and therefore bike rental decreases. The no holiday rental was 739 compared to holiday rental average of 529. 39.7% difference ((739-529)/529)x100. Regular commuting patterns may also explain this. We can't determine the cause though with this one data viz.

#Task 3
# 3.1. Load the full Seoul Bike CSV.
bikes <- read.csv(file.choose(), check.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "latin1")

# 3.2 Keep only hours when the bike rental service was operating.
bikes <- subset(bikes, `Functioning Day` == "Yes")

# 3.3 Each row represents one hour. | means OR, and & means AND.
wet_hours <- subset(bikes, `Rainfall(mm)` > 0 | `Snowfall (cm)` > 0)
both_hours <- subset(bikes, `Rainfall(mm)` > 0 & `Snowfall (cm)` > 0)

nrow(wet_hours)
nrow(both_hours)

# 3.4 Compare rain and snow separately, keeping dry hours in both plots.
rain_data <- subset(bikes, `Snowfall (cm)` == 0)
snow_data <- subset(bikes, `Rainfall(mm)` == 0)

# 3.5 cut() groups the measurements into bands.

rain_data$rain_level <- cut(
  rain_data$`Rainfall(mm)`,
  breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 1, 5, 10, Inf),
  labels = c("0", "(0, 1]", "(1, 5]", "(5, 10]", ">10")
)

snow_data$snow_level <- cut(
  snow_data$`Snowfall (cm)`,
  breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 1, 3, 5, Inf),
  labels = c("0", "(0, 1]", "(1, 3]", "(3, 5]", ">5")
)

boxplot(
  `Rented Bike Count` ~ rain_level,
  data = rain_data,
  main = "Bike rentals by rainfall level",
  xlab = "Rainfall (mm)",
  ylab = "Hourly bike rentals",
  col = "lightblue"
)

boxplot(
  `Rented Bike Count` ~ snow_level,
  data = snow_data,
  main = "Bike rentals by snowfall level",
  xlab = "Snowfall (cm)",
  ylab = "Hourly bike rentals",
  col = "lightgrey"
)

# 3.6 Check the number of hours and the median rentals in each band.
table(rain_data$rain_level)
tapply(rain_data$`Rented Bike Count`, rain_data$rain_level, median, na.rm = TRUE)

table(snow_data$snow_level)
tapply(snow_data$`Rented Bike Count`, snow_data$snow_level, median, na.rm = TRUE)
## Task 4 
```{r}
seoul_bikes |> ggplot(aes(x = temperature_c, y = humidity_percent,
                          z = rented_bike_count
                      )) + stat_summary_2d(
                        fun = mean, aes(fill
                                        = after_stat(value))
                      ) + scale_fill_viridis_c() + 
                          labs(x = "Temperature (Degrees Celsius)",
                               y = "Humidity (%)",
                               fill = "Rented Bike Count",
                               title = "Bikes Rented according to Temperature and Humidity")

```
Looking at the graph, we can see that bikes are rented most when temperature is between 20 and 25 degrees and humidity is relatively low. The sales drop off to often below 500 bikes rented per hour on average whenever temperature is below zero regardless of humidity, and there is a similar drop off when humidity nears 100% although to a less extreme extent. This implies that temperature is a greater concern when people are deciding whether or not to rent bikes, which makes intuitive sense as it is a more immediately noticeable factor.
